framework_name: ALTAI (Assessment List for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence)
creator_or_source: High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence (AI HLEG), established by the European Commission — 52 independent experts from civil society, academia, and industry across EU Member States
year_introduced: 2020 (published 17 July 2020, following a piloting process in 2019 with over 350 stakeholders; based on the 2019 Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI)
scope: Assessment — Self-assessment of AI system trustworthiness across ethical, legal, and robustness dimensions covering 7 key requirements
key_components:
ALTAI translates the AI HLEG's Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI into a practical, question-based self-assessment checklist structured around 7 key requirements. Before using ALTAI, organizations are advised to conduct a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) examining potential negative discrimination, child protection issues, data protection implications, and fundamental freedoms impacts.

**Prerequisite — Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA):** Assesses whether the AI system may negatively discriminate against protected categories (gender, ethnicity, nationality), harm children, require a Data Protection Impact Assessment, or limit fundamental freedoms such as freedom of expression.

**Requirement 1 — Human Agency and Oversight:** Assesses whether the AI system preserves human agency, supports democratic processes, and has appropriate human oversight mechanisms. Questions cover: whether the system affects fundamental rights, the level of human control (human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop, or human-in-command), availability of 'stop' buttons for safe abort, and specific oversight measures reflecting the self-learning or autonomous nature of the AI system.

**Requirement 2 — Technical Robustness and Safety:** The most extensive section, applying the precautionary principle. Questions cover: resilience to attacks and security (red-teaming, pen-testing, vulnerability assessment), fallback plans and general safety measures, risk metrics and risk levels per use case, accuracy benchmarks, reliability, and reproducibility of results. Assesses whether deliberate thought has been given to minimizing reasonably expected harms.

**Requirement 3 — Privacy and Data Governance:** Assesses data handling practices in the context of large training data volumes. Questions cover: privacy-by-design engineering, mechanisms for flagging privacy issues, privacy implications of non-personal training data, alignment with data management standards and protocols, data quality and integrity, and access controls.

**Requirement 4 — Transparency:** Organized around three themes: (1) traceability — can you trace which data was used for a given decision/recommendation; (2) explainability — have decisions been explained to users, and is the level of user understanding assessed; (3) communication — are users informed they are interacting with AI (e.g., chatbots, robo-advisors), and is the AI's capabilities and limitations disclosed.

**Requirement 5 — Diversity, Non-discrimination and Fairness:** The second most extensive section. Assesses: strategies to avoid creating or reinforcing unfair bias in input data and algorithm design, impact assessment on end-users and subjects, diversity and representativeness in training data, accessibility and universal design considerations, and stakeholder involvement from diverse backgrounds.

**Requirement 6 — Societal and Environmental Well-being:** Assesses broader societal impacts: environmental footprint of AI (energy consumption, carbon impact), impact on human work and work arrangements, effects on social relationships and democratic processes, sustainability considerations, and whether the AI system could have negative societal impact at large.

**Requirement 7 — Accountability:** Assesses governance mechanisms: processes for continual monitoring against ALTAI requirements, auditability by independent third parties, existence of an AI ethics review board, minimization and reporting of negative impacts, clear assignment of responsibility, redress mechanisms, and trade-off documentation.

The tool produces a spider diagram showing maturity across all 7 requirements plus a list of recommended improvement steps.
typical_use_case: A European company deploying an AI-powered customer service chatbot uses ALTAI before launch to systematically assess trustworthiness. The product team works through the 7 requirement sections: confirming users are informed they are talking to AI (transparency), verifying the chatbot can be overridden by human agents (human oversight), checking training data for discriminatory bias (fairness), documenting data handling practices (privacy), ensuring the system has fallback mechanisms if it fails (robustness), assessing environmental impact of compute (societal well-being), and establishing an audit trail and ethics review process (accountability). The spider diagram output reveals weak spots in explainability and bias testing, producing a prioritized remediation roadmap.
deliverables: Spider diagram visualizing maturity scores across all 7 requirements, recommended improvement actions per requirement area, completed self-assessment questionnaire documenting the organization's governance posture, gap analysis for trustworthy AI compliance readiness
genai_relevance: Medium — ALTAI was published in July 2020, before the widespread emergence of large language models and generative AI (GPT-3 had just been released). Consequently, it does not explicitly address GenAI-specific concerns such as hallucination, prompt injection, training data copyright, synthetic content labelling, or foundation model supply chain accountability. However, the 7 requirements remain broadly applicable to GenAI systems: transparency questions apply to chatbot disclosure, fairness questions apply to LLM bias, robustness questions apply to adversarial attacks on models, and accountability questions apply to model audit trails. Several 2024 academic papers (notably Lee 2024 in ACM) have applied ALTAI's framework specifically to assess LLM ethical risks, demonstrating it can serve as a starting point even for GenAI projects, though it needs supplementation with GenAI-specific assessment criteria.
accessibility_for_non_engineers: High — ALTAI was specifically designed to be intuitive and understandable after feedback from the piloting process with 350+ organizations. Questions are phrased in plain language with pro-active wording. The web-based tool at altai.insight-centre.org guides users through multiple-choice and text-based questions without requiring technical expertise. The checklist format is familiar to business professionals. Non-engineers can meaningfully complete most sections, particularly those on human oversight, transparency, societal well-being, and accountability. Technical robustness and privacy sections may require input from engineering staff, but the questions themselves are accessible.
time_to_apply: Half-day to full-day workshop (2-6 hours) for a single AI system assessment, depending on organizational size and the complexity of the AI system. The revised ALTAI was specifically shortened from its predecessor to reduce effort. For organizations new to AI ethics, initial completion may take longer as it raises awareness questions the team may not have previously considered. Ongoing reassessment is recommended as the system evolves.
free_or_paid: Free — The ALTAI PDF is freely downloadable from the European Commission website, and the interactive web-based tool at altai.insight-centre.org is free to use. No consulting or paid subscription required. The underlying Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI are also freely available.
adoption_level: Widely adopted — ALTAI is the official self-assessment tool from the European Commission's AI HLEG and has been widely referenced in EU policy documents, academic research (cited by 72+ papers as of the Radclyffe et al. 2023 review), and industry governance frameworks. It has been piloted by 350+ organizations during its development. It is recognized as a complementary governance tool alongside the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, and ISO 42001 in systematic reviews of AI governance frameworks. However, actual voluntary adoption by industry beyond the pilot remains uncertain, as there is no mandatory requirement to use it and no public reporting of ALTAI scores.
ai_project_stage: Multiple — Primarily serves PoC, MVP, and Production stages. The FRIA and initial ALTAI assessment should ideally be conducted during the design phase (PoC/MVP) before deployment. However, it can be applied at any stage including to already-deployed systems to identify governance gaps. Recommended as an ongoing process with periodic reassessment during Maintenance and Scale stages as the system evolves.
relevance_for_entrepreneurs: ALTAI provides startup founders with a structured, free, EU-endorsed methodology to demonstrate AI trustworthiness to investors, customers, and regulators. Key value: (1) Investor readiness — completing an ALTAI assessment signals governance maturity to VCs increasingly focused on responsible AI; (2) Pre-regulatory compliance — ALTAI's 7 requirements map closely to the EU AI Act's trustworthiness concepts, making it valuable preparation for upcoming compliance obligations; (3) De-risking — as noted in the Radclyffe et al. review, completing ALTAI can substantially de-risk an organization by providing documented evidence of governance practices; (4) Trust-building — the spider diagram creates a tangible, shareable artifact showing governance posture to partners and customers; (5) Gap identification — reveals blind spots in AI governance before they become costly compliance failures or PR incidents. The tool is particularly valuable because it is free, does not require consultants, and carries the authority of the European Commission.
session_mapping: S5 (Ethics/Governance) — Primary session for hands-on ALTAI self-assessment workshop. Also relevant to S3 (Projects) for integrating trustworthiness assessment into AI project management methodology.
complements: Pairs naturally with the EU AI Act Risk Classification (ALTAI was the precursor assessment tool; its 7 requirements map closely to the Act's trustworthiness framework and it serves as practical preparation for compliance). Complements NIST AI RMF (ALTAI's checklist approach is more prescriptive where NIST provides a broader risk management methodology — using both covers governance and operational risk). Works well with AI Project Canvas or Machine Learning Canvas (use the canvas for project scoping, then ALTAI for ethics/governance assessment). Complements ISO 42001 (ALTAI identifies gaps that ISO 42001's management system structure can operationalize).
limitations: Key limitations identified by academic reviews (Radclyffe et al. 2023, Rajamaki 2023): (1) No risk differentiation — ALTAI applies the same standard regardless of the risk level of the AI system (a spam filter and a medical diagnostic tool get the same assessment), unlike the EU AI Act's risk-tiered approach; (2) Self-assessment bias — as a self-assessment tool, there is no independent verification, and organizations may overstate their governance maturity; (3) No peer comparison — scores are absolute rather than relative to industry peers, making it difficult to benchmark and potentially discouraging for early-stage startups that score poorly despite being appropriate for their maturity level; (4) FRIA not integrated — the Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment is recommended as a prerequisite but is not built into the tool or reflected in the final score; (5) Pre-GenAI design — published before ChatGPT and the GenAI revolution, missing questions specific to foundation models, hallucination, synthetic content, and LLM supply chains; (6) Scoring opacity — the weighting of each question's contribution to the spider diagram scores is not transparent to users; (7) No enforcement mechanism — completion is entirely voluntary with no regulatory consequence for non-adoption.
example_application: A French health-tech startup, 'DiagAssist AI', is developing an AI system that assists dermatologists in detecting skin cancer from patient photos. Before seeking CE marking and clinical validation, the CTO leads a half-day ALTAI workshop with the product team, a data protection officer, and a medical ethics advisor. They work through the 7 requirements: (Req 1) Confirm human oversight — dermatologists always make final diagnosis, AI only flags suspicious lesions; (Req 2) Technical robustness — document accuracy benchmarks across skin tones, red-team for adversarial image attacks; (Req 3) Privacy — verify GDPR-compliant patient data handling, anonymization of training images; (Req 4) Transparency — ensure the system explains why it flagged a lesion (explainability) and that patients know AI assisted their diagnosis; (Req 5) Fairness — test for bias across skin tones and demographics in training data; (Req 6) Societal well-being — assess impact on dermatologist workload and patient access to care; (Req 7) Accountability — establish an AI ethics review board, plan for independent auditing. The spider diagram reveals a gap in fairness testing (limited training data diversity for darker skin tones), prompting the team to prioritize dataset expansion before launch.
available_templates: ALTAI interactive web tool (free): https://altai.insight-centre.org/ | ALTAI PDF checklist download (free, from European Commission): https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/document.cfm?doc_id=68342 | ALTAI on EU Futurium platform: https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/european-ai-alliance/document/ai-hleg-assessment-list-trustworthy-artificial-intelligence-altai | Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI (underlying framework): https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/ethics-guidelines-trustworthy-ai
regulatory_alignment: EU AI Act (ALTAI's 7 requirements directly influenced and align with the EU AI Act's trustworthiness framework — the AI HLEG's work was a key input to the Act's development), GDPR (privacy and data governance requirement maps to GDPR obligations), EU Charter of Fundamental Rights (the FRIA prerequisite directly references the Charter)
